title: Choirs

segments.voice: Yesterday, organs, guitars and drums, and a psalm that ends on breath. Your line was every instrument praise. Which ordinary sound did you hear as part of the list? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-six.

Four people stand in a row, and each one sings a different note. On its own, the low note sounds gloomy. The high one sounds thin. The two in the middle sound like they've lost the tune. Then they sing at the same moment, and the four odd notes become one chord, full and warm, that none of them could make alone. That's the whole secret of a choir. It's there in a cathedral choir in white robes, in a gospel choir swaying on the beat, in an Orthodox choir singing a service from start to finish, and in a village church where six faithful people stand up every week. Today: choirs.

Start at the temple. When Solomon's temple is dedicated, the book of Chronicles describes the musicians this way: "It came even to pass, as the trumpeters and singers were as one, to make one sound to be heard in praising and thanking the LORD." As one, to make one sound. And the story says that then the house was filled with a cloud. The singing comes first, and the glory follows it. Next, one mouth, many voices. Paul writes to the Christians in Rome: "That ye may with one mind and one mouth glorify God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ." One mouth sounds like everyone saying the same thing. But a choir shows another way. Sopranos, altos, tenors and basses each sing a different line, and the unity is in the harmony, not in sameness. If everyone sang the melody, you'd lose the chord. Then, a choir on a wall. In the book of Nehemiah, the broken walls of Jerusalem have been rebuilt, and Nehemiah sets up two great companies of singers giving thanks. One goes one way along the top of the wall, the other goes the opposite way, and they meet at the house of God. Two choirs, walking around a city, singing it back to life. Last, a scene near the Bible's end. In Revelation, John hears heaven, and it sounds like a choir: "And I heard as it were the voice of a great multitude, and as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of mighty thunderings, saying, Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth." Many waters: countless voices, each its own, poured into one sound. In this scene, heaven doesn't whisper. It sings.

Here's the practice: sing with others. If someone's with you, hum a simple tune together, a hymn, a lullaby, anything you both know. Don't worry about sounding good. Listen for the moment your voices meet. If you're alone, put on a recording of a choir and hum along with one part, the low one or the high one, and notice how your single line fits inside the whole. If you pray, you can let the song be your prayer, sung alongside other voices. If you don't, just listen for the place where many voices become one sound. The bell holds the time.
Choirs. Many voices, each holding its own part, making one sound to praise God.

Your line: many voices. Today, in one group you're part of, at work, at home, online, listen for the different parts people play, and how they make one sound. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Church choirs come in different forms: robed cathedral and parish choirs, gospel choirs, Orthodox choirs that sing the whole liturgy, and small groups of volunteers who rehearse during the week and lead the congregation's singing on Sunday.

pairs: as one, to make one sound

sopranos, altos, tenors and basses each sing a different line. the unity is in the harmony.
at the temple, the singers were 'as one, to make one sound'
and Chronicles says the house was then filled with a cloud.
in Revelation 19, John hears heaven as one lone voice
he hears "the voice of a great multitude, and as the voice of many waters," saying Alleluia.

fork.setup: you're Nehemiah. Jerusalem's walls are rebuilt, and it's time to give thanks. how do you arrange the singers?
options: one big crowd at the main gate.
two great companies, walking the wall in opposite directions.
a single singer on the highest tower.
fork.reveal: two companies giving thanks set off in opposite directions along the wall and met at the house of God.

trapdoor: what you thought: a choir is the people who sing so the rest don't have to.
what it means: many different voices, each holding its own part, making one sound.
what a scholar hears: Chronicles: the singers "as one, to make one sound," and then the house filled with a cloud. the song comes before the glory.
recall: Catholic and Orthodox word for it

notes: Audit: 'Revelation's heaven is not silent' and the myth 'Revelation pictures heaven as silent' (false) were contradicted by Revelation 8:1 ('there was silence in heaven about the space of half an hour'); the teach now speaks of this scene only, and the myth item is about Revelation 19's multitude.
Editor pass: 'Revelation pictures the end' changed, since Revelation 19:6 is a scene of heaven, not the story's end.
Nehemiah 12:31–40 summarized: two thanksgiving companies on the wall, going opposite ways, meeting at the house of God; confirm the summary.
'Revelation pictures the end not in silence, but in song. generalizes from Revelation 19; a Keeper may prefer 'Revelation pictures'.
Hook's list of choir kinds (cathedral, gospel, Orthodox, a village church) is illustrative and unquantified.
Original left null: the Greek choros was avoided under the claims rule (it would invite an etymology of 'choir').
